sections.overview: The brown shrimp, or common shrimp, is a small crustacean of European shallow coasts that buries itself in sand and is fished commercially. It is one of the most abundant animals of sandy bays and estuaries, and a key food for fish and wading birds.
sections.identification: The body is long, thin and mottled brown, slightly flattened from top to bottom, and its colour matches the sediment. The rostrum is short and blunt, the first walking leg is subchelate (a small hook-like claw), and the telson has two pairs of lateral spines. Females grow larger than males, with a reported maximum of about 8.5–9.5 cm, rarely reached. A reliable adult body-mass range was not found in the consulted sources; reported size is chiefly given as total length and varies with sex and population.
sections.habitat: It lives on sandy and muddy bottoms from the intertidal zone to about 150 m deep, in open coast, estuaries, lagoons and bays, and prefers sediment with grains of 125–710 µm. Its range runs along European coasts from the White Sea to Morocco, and into the Mediterranean and Black Seas. It tolerates a very wide range of salinity.
sections.diet: It is an omnivorous predator and scavenger that forages mostly at night. It eats polychaete worms, small fish, molluscs, small crustaceans and green seaweeds such as sea lettuce. Newly settled juveniles rely on the annual bloom of copepods.
sections.behavior: The shrimp buries itself in 9–10 seconds by beating its abdominal limbs and sweeping sand over its back, leaving only the eyes and antennae out, to hide from predators and ambush prey. It can swim, crawl or walk. Adults move offshore from November to March to avoid low-salinity water, and young shrimps use inshore nurseries for a few weeks.
sections.reproduction: Breeding is spread over much of the year, with summer eggs (up to 4,500 per female) and larger winter eggs (up to 2,800) produced from October–November; females carry them for 4 to 13 weeks depending on temperature. Planktonic larvae live 1 to 6 months, and juveniles settle from May to July. Maturity comes at 35–50 mm, and whether the species changes sex is debated.
sections.ecology: Gulls, terns, redshanks, cod relatives, flatfish, gurnards and young bass eat brown shrimps, which can reach about 60 per square metre in summer peaks. Most individuals are in their first year class; the maximum age reported is about 3 years in one source and up to 5 in females in another. Black spot shell disease affects between 13% and 87% of shrimps in British sites.
sections.conservation: No conservation category was found in the sources read. European landings rose from about 5,000 t in 1950 to nearly 29,000 t in 1997, taken mainly by beam trawl; about half of a catch is undersized. High fecundity and fast turnover let populations recover quickly.
